item.title: AI Dev Tool Risks: Cursor/Codex Escapes, JadePuffer EncForge, FakeGit, HuggingFace Breach
item.content:encoded:
A Look Inside the HuggingFace Breach — Must Read

HuggingFace disclosed a breach where an autonomous AI attacker exploited RCE flaws in its dataset processing pipeline to steal credentials and move laterally, while defenders used AI-driven detection to investigate and contain it. The key takeaway is that AI/ML workloads and downloaded datasets must be treated as untrusted code with strict least privilege and monitoring for unusual access patterns.

  • On July 16, 2026, HuggingFace disclosed a security breach in which an autonomous AI attacker infiltrated its internal infrastructure.
  • The attacker exploited two remote code execution vulnerabilities in HuggingFace’s dataset processing pipeline, including abuse of a remote-code dataset loader and template injection in a dataset configuration.
  • The attacker leaked cloud and cluster credentials, moved laterally into several internal clusters, and generated decoy activity to complicate attribution and impact analysis.
  • HuggingFace detected the compromise with an AI-assisted threat detection system and used LLM-driven analysis agents to extract indicators of compromise from logs.
  • HuggingFace recommended that users rotate API access tokens and report any unusual account activity.

JadePuffer agentic attacks now target AI model data with ransomware — Must Read

JadePuffer has evolved its autonomous ransomware attacks with EncForge, malware designed to encrypt AI and ML assets such as model checkpoints, training datasets, and vector databases. Sysdig says the latest intrusion abused a vulnerable Langflow instance and exposed Docker socket, underscoring the need to patch Langflow and lock down AI infrastructure.

  • JadePuffer has upgraded with custom malware called EncForge that focuses on encrypting AI assets such as training datasets, vector databases, and model checkpoints.
  • Sysdig said the attacker returned to a previously breached Langflow instance vulnerable to CVE-2025-3248 and discovered an exposed Docker socket that provided root-level control.
  • When the initial ransomware download failed, the operator developed and deployed six Python scripts over five minutes, with the final deploy.py v2 solving the delivery issues.
  • EncForge targets approximately 180 file extensions across AI and machine learning infrastructure, including Hugging Face SafeTensors files, PyTorch and TensorFlow models, GGUF and GGML weights, FAISS indexes, and training datasets.
  • Sysdig found no evidence that JadePuffer exfiltrated data during the intrusion, and EncForge itself does not appear to include a data-stealing mechanism.

FakeGit Campaign Uses 7,600 GitHub Repositories to Spread SmartLoader Malware — Must Read

Researchers found a FakeGit campaign using about 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories, including fake AI skills and MCP servers, to trick users or AI agents into downloading SmartLoader, which can deploy the StealC info-stealer. The key risk is that AI agents can independently discover these convincing repositories and pass along attacker-supplied installation instructions, making vetted plugin catalogs and sandboxing essential.

  • Researchers discovered nearly 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories in the FakeGit campaign, with more than 800 posing as AI skills or Model Context Protocol servers.
  • FakeGit uses copied projects, lookalike developer profiles, convincing README files, and malicious ZIP files to deliver SmartLoader malware.
  • SmartLoader is used to establish persistence and deploy secondary payloads such as the StealC information stealer.
  • Island reported that Anthropic Claude Code, Google Gemini, and OpenAI ChatGPT could surface malicious campaign repositories without being shown a link.
  • The counterfeit repositories lead users or AI agents through setup instructions that trigger a LuaJIT loader chain and drop SmartLoader, which can then deploy StealC.

Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity hit by sandbox escapes — Should Read

Researchers found sandbox escapes in Cursor, OpenAI Codex CLI, Google Gemini CLI, and Antigravity where AI agents could write trusted workspace files that outside tools later executed or loaded, enabling host-level code execution. Most issues have been patched, but the findings show a broader design risk in AI coding agents that trust project files too much.

  • Pillar Security researchers reproduced sandbox escapes in Cursor, OpenAI's Codex, Google's Gemini CLI, and Antigravity by having agents write files that trusted tools outside the sandbox later ran, loaded, or scanned.
  • The article says prompt injection can trigger these escapes when malicious instructions are planted in places such as a README, issue, dependency, or diff and become local actions on a developer's machine.
  • Pillar Security grouped the seven findings into four failure modes: denylist sandboxes, executable workspace configuration, unsafe command allowlists, and privileged local daemons outside the sandbox.
  • Most of the issues are patched and vendor-acknowledged, including Cursor fixes in version 3.0.0 and an OpenAI Codex CLI fix in version 0.95.0.
  • Google classified the two Antigravity findings as “Other valid security vulnerabilities” and downgraded them because it judged them difficult to exploit due to the need for social engineering or a trusted repository carrying an indirect prompt injection.

India says allegedly leaked nuclear plant files pose no safety risk — Should Read

India’s nuclear operator said files allegedly leaked by World Leaks from a Reliance Infrastructure contractor breach relate only to non-nuclear support infrastructure at the Kudankulam plant and do not affect nuclear safety or security. The incident highlights third-party exposure rather than a confirmed compromise of reactor or operational systems.

  • India's Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited said documents recently posted online and allegedly linked to the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant contain no information affecting nuclear safety or security.
  • The files published by World Leaks appeared to include engineering drawings, supplier information, inspection records, and insurance documents related to Kudankulam Units 3 and 4, which are under construction.
  • Reliance Group said it suffered a partial breach involving data stored on infrastructure hosted by Indian data center provider Yotta, while Yotta said it detected and stopped suspicious activity on a Reliance Infrastructure server in late May.
  • Independent researcher Rakesh Krishnan said nearly 19,000 Kudankulam-related files totaling about 14.3 GB were published by World Leaks on June 11, but the authenticity of the documents could not be independently verified.
  • World Leaks emerged in early 2025 after Hunters International rebranded and has increasingly focused on stealing and publishing data to pressure victims into paying extortion demands.

Flock Safety kills acoustic system designed to detect 'human distress' — May Read

Flock Safety is dropping its limited-trial acoustic “Distress Detection” system after privacy advocates objected to its ability to detect screams and other human distress sounds. The company says the system could not understand speech or identify voices and cited community consultation for the decision.

  • Flock Safety is abandoning plans to sell an acoustic gunshot detection device that could detect screaming and other types of “human distress.”
  • Flock disclosed on July 10 that it had decided to remove the product, saying the decision followed community consultation.
  • The company said the feature was only available to a small number of customers in a limited trial and was never broadly released.
  • Flock said the system cannot understand speech, analyze language, or identify voices.
  • The Electronic Frontier Foundation criticized the feature over civil liberties concerns, the possibility of summoning armed police to loud street interactions, and potential illegality under some state eavesdropping laws.
